name: Traveling with cannabis: flights, airports and borders
where_it_stands: Carrying marijuana across state lines or onto a plane remains a federal offense, even between two legal states. TSA changed its website listing for medical marijuana in April 2026, but says its policy has not changed: officers do not search for drugs, yet they refer any marijuana they find to law enforcement.
summary: Federal law makes simple possession of marijuana a crime nationwide, with up to a year in prison and a minimum $1,000 fine for a first offense; the Congressional Research Service says that penalty is unchanged by rescheduling, though the April 2026 order appears to let certified medical patients possess state-licensed product. TSA's guidance says marijuana and some CBD products remain illegal federally except products with no more than 0.3% THC or FDA-approved drugs, that its screening looks for security threats rather than drugs, and that officers must report suspected violations to police. In late April 2026 TSA's 'What Can I Bring?' tool switched its medical marijuana entry from 'No' to 'Yes (Special Instructions)'; a TSA spokesperson told NORML the policy itself had not changed. What happens after a referral depends on local police at the airport. Driving across state lines with cannabis is likewise federally illegal, and legal states still regulate it in cars, from sealed-container rules in Illinois to bans on in-vehicle use. International travel is riskier: even rescheduled medical marijuana needs a DEA permit to be imported or exported under the April 2026 order, and a 2018 CBP statement, as summarized by immigration lawyers, said Canadians working in their country's legal cannabis industry may be refused entry if their trip relates to that work.

what_changes.text: Buying legally at your destination is safer than flying or driving cannabis across state lines, which remains a federal offense regardless of state law.
A medical card does not authorize interstate transport, and the TSA website change offers no legal protection, according to NORML.
Hemp products under 0.3% THC are federally lawful today, but those rules tighten on 11 December 2026 and some states ban products others allow.

timeline.event: TSA's website changes its medical marijuana listing to 'Yes (Special Instructions)' without changing policy
State-licensed medical marijuana moves to Schedule III; federal possession penalties unchanged
Tighter federal hemp definition takes effect, affecting which hemp products travelers can carry

faq.a: Federal law still prohibits it. TSA does not search for drugs, but if officers find marijuana they refer it to police, and outcomes vary by airport.

faq.q: Can I fly with medical marijuana?
faq.a: TSA's site now shows 'Yes (Special Instructions)', but TSA says its policy has not changed, and a card does not authorize carrying marijuana across state lines.

faq.q: Can I drive cannabis between two legal states?
faq.a: No. Interstate transport is federally illegal even between legal states.
TSA says products with no more than 0.3% THC or FDA-approved drugs are not federally illegal, but items that look or smell like marijuana may still prompt a police referral.
